```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "A has a clearer path to a first payment. The buyer is named (municipal IT director, webmaster or clerk), the universe is enumerable, and the brief describes a purchase route that skips an RFP: micro-purchases under about $10,000. Competitors publish prices of $29 to $349 per month aimed at that route, which gives a concrete price anchor.",
    "B's price anchors are weaker. Nalvis is pre-launch or waitlist-only, Since.dev's Pro price is not disclosed, mendapi's hosted tier has no price, and three other entrants' pricing is NOT FOUND. Several rivals also give away their core engine as free open source, which pushes against the $14 to $150 per month hypothesis.",
    "B carries a trust barrier that a solo operator struggles to clear within 90 days. Customers must grant PR-opening access to production code, and the brief itself says SOC 2 Type II or equivalent is commonly expected before that. A's scan-and-report product needs no access to customer systems.",
    "A's acquisition costs are quantified: $1,300 to $1,800 per municipal league booth and $250 to $7,500 per sponsorship. Those venues concentrate the exact buyer. B's channels (GitHub Marketplace, dev.to, Product Hunt) are cheap, but they reach developers broadly rather than a buyer with budget authority.",
    "Both markets are crowded, with 6 to 7 near-identical entrants each, so crowding does not separate them. A's brief also flags a possible opening: several competitors still show the stale April 2026 deadline, which leaves room for accurate, trust-building messaging."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence rests on three dev.to posts. At least one ('How Stripe silently broke my production app and how I built a fix') is written by a builder promoting their own solution rather than by a prospective buyer. None of the three shows willingness to pay, and the price anchors come from products that are pre-launch, waitlist-only, or have undisclosed pricing.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. A has serious weaknesses of its own. The DOJ's April 2026 extension to 2027/2028 undercuts urgency. The field is commoditized. Its demand evidence is thin: one industry quote, one vendor marketing claim included only as directional, and an NLC survey. Liability from overselling automated scans is also real. Neither brief shows verified paying customers for any competitor. A wins mainly because its payer, purchase route and price are more concrete, and because B's code-access trust and SOC 2 requirements are harder to clear in 90 days."
}
```
